A fly brain, playing music

Twenty seconds of audio pushed through the Drosophila male CNS connectome — 165,122 neurons, 15 million synapses — simulated as spiking neurons. Sound enters at the antennae; descending-neuron spikes come out as notes.

The positions are real. Every dot sits where that neuron sits in the imaged fly, and lights when that neuron fired. One simplification: the dot marks the cell body, and a fly neuron often computes far from its cell body, out along its branches. The 86 antennal cells are the exception — their somata sit in the antenna, outside the scan, so they are drawn at their axon terminals in the brain, which is where they deliver the sound.

The melody is not the fly's. Each voice is one anatomical family of descending neurons, and its pitch was assigned by name order before any audio was played. What the fly supplies is the timing. Sound reaches these neurons across a single synapse; two synapses in, the signal is at chance — which is why the deep cells barely flicker.
